H7 only partly holds. Customers pay late year after year, but outside two large customers the lateness is spread across the whole customer base rather than sitting with a few accounts. I saved `prediction.json`, `notes.md` and `finding.json` (F3, medium confidence).

**What holds:**
- **It's real lateness, not a date artefact.** For the 69,850 invoices dated 2016–2024 (265 customers, all paid), amount-weighted days past due average 18.11. 68.3% of invoices were paid after their due date. The working-day due date actually falls 0.23 days later than the calendar terms on average, so it doesn't inflate the figure (q110).
- **The money:** about $1,413,693 more receivables than terms imply, which is $113,095/yr at an 8% cost of capital. The 8% rate is my assumption, not from the records (q139).
- **It persists by customer.** A customer's lateness one year correlates 0.80–0.95 with the next. That's for customers with at least 30 invoices in both years, 14–25 of them per pair (q124).
- **Customers 7 and 6 are the outliers.** Both are on 30-day terms. They paid 26–42 days late in every year, against 11–23 days for everyone else combined. Together they carry 0.28–0.44 of overdue dollar-days on 0.16–0.27 of billing (q119). Their median invoice is 24 days late; everyone else's is 2 (q142).

**What doesn't hold:**
- **Concentration mostly mirrors revenue.** The top 10 customers carry 71.6% of overdue dollar-days, but they also bill 67.6% of revenue (q112).
- **Most of the money is a broad tail.** 75% of overdue dollar-days come from invoices more than 30 days late (q120). Outside customers 6 and 7, about 20% of invoices are that late (q144). Among the 30 customers with at least 200 invoices, that share varies from customer to customer but has nothing to do with how big the customer is.
- **Short payments are not concentrated in the late payers.** They total $167,868 over nine years, and the customers averaging over 30 days late hold 17.7% of those dollars on 22.8% of billing (q129, q136).
- **Invoice size and month make no difference** (q132).
- **2022 was high for everyone.** The peak was in 2022-H1 across 167 customers, and it was back to normal by 2023-H1 (q147).

**What that means for recovery:** if customers 6 and 7 paid at the pace of everyone else, about $270,734 of cash would be freed, worth $21,659/yr at 8% (q139). The rest of the excess is spread across accounts. That points to a general collections step, such as a reminder after the due date, rather than chasing a few customers.

**What the records can't tell:** why customers 6 and 7 pay late. Their steady ~24-day lag could be their own payment calendar, invoices reaching them late, or deliberate stretching. The data has no dispute, invoice-receipt or collection-history fields. Asking whether they have agreed terms other than net 30 is the next step.
